content: Flank pain is defined as discomfort or distress experienced in the posterior region or along the midaxillary line, below the ribs and above the iliac crest. This pain is often caused by distension of the renal capsule, which stimulates specialized nerve endings. Flank pain originating from urinary tract pathology may result from underlying obstruction, inflammation, or the presence of a mass. Common urologic causes include renal calculi (kidney stones) and acute pyelonephritis, but other potential causes such as cardiac, intra-abdominal, musculoskeletal, or psychological factors should also be considered. The kidney and its capsule are innervated by sensory fibers that travel to the T10-L1 spinal cord levels. Consequently, pain from the kidney is typically felt just lateral to the sacrospinalis muscle, beneath the 12th rib posteriorly. This pain often radiates anteriorly and may be referred to the inguinal, labial, penile, or testicular regions. The quality and severity of the pain can provide diagnostic clues, as the intensity of the pain often inversely correlates with the duration of the underlying condition. For example, dull and steady pain is indicative of infectious causes like acute pyelonephritis, whereas sharp and intense pain is characteristic of an acutely obstructing renal calculus. Mild to moderate flank pain may be associated with conditions such as a slowly enlarging ureteral tumor, which causes chronic, gradual distension of the renal collecting system and capsule over time. Conversely, acute flank pain due to an obstructing renal calculus, known as renal colic, is typically severe and sharp, resulting from sudden distension of the renal collecting system and capsule. It is critical to determine whether the pain represents an emergency condition requiring immediate intervention or can be managed in an outpatient setting. Flank pain accompanied by fever, dehydration, nausea, vomiting, or comorbid conditions such as diabetes, immunosuppression, or pregnancy may necessitate hospital admission to prevent complications such as pyelonephritis, urosepsis, or renal failure. Pathophysiology of Flank Pain Flank pain originating from the urinary system is primarily caused by distension of the ureter, renal pelvis, or renal capsule. The severity of the pain is directly related to the rapidity or acuteness of the obstruction, regardless of the degree of distension. Acute Onset: Patients with acute obstruction, such as a stone lodged in the ureter, experience extremely severe pain even with mild ureteral dilation. As the stone moves and becomes lodged in different positions, it can cause multiple episodes of severe pain. Chronic Onset: Chronic ureteral dilation, which develops over a long period, may result in severe obstruction and irreversible renal damage but is often associated with little to no pain. The location of the pain can help predict the level of obstruction in the urinary tract: Proximal Ureteral or Renal Pelvic Obstruction: Pain originates in the posterior flank and radiates to the ipsilateral testicle in males or the labia in females due to shared innervation (T11–T12). Middle Third of the Ureter: Pain gradually becomes lower and more anterior in the flank. Ureterovesical Junction Obstruction: Pain is lower and radiates to the scrotal skin rather than the testicle and is often associated with urinary frequency and urgency. Renal Stone Formation Renal stone formation involves two primary processes: urine supersaturation and physicochemical changes. Urine Supersaturation: Low urine volumes (less than 1 liter per day) increase solute concentration (indicated by urine osmolarity >600 mOsm/kg) and promote urinary stasis, leading to solute supersaturation and stone formation. Solutes precipitate in the urine, resulting in nucleation and crystal formation. Risk factors for nephrolithiasis include supersaturation of stone-forming constituents such as calcium, phosphorus, uric acid, oxalate, and cystine, as well as low urine volume. Physicochemical Changes: Urine pH and the concentration of specific substances influence the transformation of solutes from liquid to solid. Most urinary stones begin as Randall’s plaques at the junction of the nephron’s collecting tubule and the renal pelvis in the papilla. These plaques grow suburothelially and eventually break through into the renal pelvis, where layers of calcium oxalate form on a calcium phosphate nidus. Calcium phosphate stones form in alkaline urine, while overly acidic urine predisposes to uric acid stones. Metabolic disturbances such as hyperparathyroidism and renal tubular acidosis are associated with calcium phosphate stones. Acute Pyelonephritis Acute pyelonephritis is most commonly caused by Escherichia coli due to its ability to adhere to and colonize the urinary tract and kidneys. E. coli possesses adhesive molecules called P-fimbriae, which interact with receptors on uroepithelial cells. Infection of the kidneys by E. coli can trigger an acute inflammatory response, potentially leading to scarring of the renal parenchyma. The mechanism of renal scarring is not fully understood but may involve bacterial adhesion disrupting protective barriers, resulting in localized infection, hypoxia, ischemia, and clotting. Inflammatory cytokines and bacterial toxins can exacerbate the condition, leading to complete pyelonephritis and, in severe cases, systemic symptoms of sepsis and shock. Causes of Flank Pain The etiology of flank pain is multifactorial, ranging from local, systemic, and metabolic causes to underlying genetic factors. Depending on the cause and associated comorbidities, patients may require treatment in an outpatient or hospital setting. Life-threatening causes, if left untreated, can result in death or permanent renal disability within 24 hours. Epidemiology and Demographics Renal Colic: Nephrolithiasis affects 5–15% of the population, with 50% experiencing recurrent stones within 5–7 years if preventive measures are not taken. Stones are more common in individuals aged 20–50 years and occur twice as frequently in men as in women. Acute Pyelonephritis: This condition is reported at a rate of 15–17 cases per 10,000 females and 3–4 cases per 10,000 males annually in the United States. Risk factors include extremes of age, anatomical abnormalities, hormonal changes, sexual activity, and pregnancy. Renal Infarction: Renal artery thrombosis is typically seen in individuals aged 30–50 years, with no gender predominance. It is often underdiagnosed, leading to a falsely low documented incidence. Risk Factors Risk factors for flank pain include primary factors related to the urinary system and secondary conditions arising from extra-urinary pathologies. These factors predispose patients to flank pain and its associated complications. Screening Prenatal renal ultrasound is used to identify renal anomalies, exclude associated malformations, and predict postnatal renal function. Conditions such as unilateral renal agenesis, ectopic kidneys, obstructive dysplasia, multicystic kidney disease, nephroblastomatosis, renal vein thrombosis, and others can be detected. Early detection allows for prenatal counseling, therapeutic intervention, and postnatal management. Prognosis Nephrolithiasis: Most kidney stones pass within four weeks, but stones larger than 8 mm may require intervention. Recurrence is common, with 30–50% of individuals experiencing another stone within 10 years. Adequate fluid intake and dietary modifications are essential for prevention. Urinary Tract Infection (UTI): Most women have excellent outcomes, with symptom resolution within 2–4 days of antibiotic treatment. However, 30% may experience recurrence. Morbidity is higher in older, debilitated patients and those with comorbidities such as diabetes or chronic catheterization. Complications Acute Pyelonephritis: Complications include renal or perinephric abscess, sepsis, renal vein thrombosis, papillary necrosis, acute renal failure, and emphysematous pyelonephritis. Renal Calculi: Complications include abscess formation, urosepsis, ureteral scarring or perforation, urine extravasation, and kidney atrophy in chronic cases. Flank Pain in Reproductive-Aged and Pregnant Females In reproductive-aged females, gynecologic and obstetric causes such as ectopic pregnancy, ovarian cysts, ovarian torsion, and pelvic inflammatory disease should be considered. Diagnostic workup in premenopausal women must include a beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG) test to avoid exposing a fetus to ionizing radiation. Ultrasound and MRI are preferred imaging modalities during pregnancy due to their safety.
